name: Label AI-generated content and log disclosures for the EU AI Act

parameters.content:
## Label AI-generated content for the EU AI Act

Article 50 of the EU AI Act has applied since 2 August 2026. It was not moved
by the Digital Omnibus that delayed the high-risk rules to 2027. If you
publish AI-generated images, video, audio or text into the EU, you owe a
disclosure now, and you need to be able to show you made it.

### How it works

Drop an AI-generated file into a Drive folder. The file is downloaded and
hashed with SHA-256, so the record points at one exact version rather than a
file name that can change. Its type decides which duty applies: synthetic
images, video and audio always carry the machine-readable marking duty, while
whether the same file is a deepfake of a real person is a judgement a mime
type cannot make. The workflow separates what it can decide from what it
cannot, and only the second kind is held for a person. A readable disclosure
manifest is written as JSON and saved next to the asset, carrying the visible
label, the duties identified, the hash and a schema.org block a publishing
system can read. Everything lands in a register with the reviewer, the status
and the timestamps. Files needing no judgement move straight to the approved
folder; the rest wait, and an hourly sweep moves each one once a reviewer sets
its row to Signed off, writing who signed and when.

### Setup

Connect Drive, Sheets and Gmail. Create the review and approved folders, fill
the Settings row, and create the Register tab with the columns named on that
node.

### Note

This produces a disclosure record, not legal advice. Have your own counsel
confirm which duties apply to you.

## Pick up the file and fingerprint it
A new file in the review folder is downloaded and hashed with SHA-256, so the register points at one exact version rather than a file name that can be changed later.

## Work out the duty, write the manifest
The asset type decides which part of Article 50 applies. A readable JSON manifest with the label, duties, hash and a schema.org block is saved next to the asset.

## Register it, then route it
Every file gets a register row. Those needing no human judgement move straight to approved. The rest wait, and the reviewer is emailed what to confirm.

## Release what has been signed off
An hourly sweep moves each file whose row a reviewer set to Signed off, once only, and writes back who signed and when.

nodes.name: New File In The Review Folder
nodes.notes: Drop AI-generated files into this folder. Everything that lands here is treated as synthetic output and gets a disclosure record.

nodes.name: Read Disclosure Settings
nodes.notes: Settings tab, one row: Organisation, Role (provider or deployer), Generation Tool, Label Wording, Publishes Public Interest Content (yes or no), Reviewer Email

nodes.name: Hash The File
nodes.notes: A SHA-256 of the bytes ties the register entry to one exact file. Without it a register says a disclosure happened but not for which version.

nodes.name: Save The Manifest Beside The Asset
Write The Disclosure Register Row
nodes.notes: Register tab columns: Register ID, Detected At, File Name, File ID, Mime Type, Size Bytes, Content SHA256, Asset Kind, Duties, Visible Label, Manifest File ID, Needs Sign Off, Status, Reviewer, Signed Off By, Signed Off At, Published At, Moved

nodes.name: Does A Person Need To Look?
Ask The Reviewer To Sign Off
